strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant gap: existing representation alignment work is almost entirely pairwise, leading to O(M^2) scaling and no guarantee of cycle consistency when M≥3 models are involved. The paper clearly articulates why a shared 'universe' factorization is preferable.

The empirical evaluation is broad, spanning probing/stitching (CIFAR-100), clustering (MASSIVE), multilingual retrieval (TED-Multi), cross-camera re-identification (Market-1501), and cross-modal retrieval (Flickr8k), which gives reasonable evidence that the proposed GCPA method is useful across diverse settings and modalities.

The 'weak-link healing' experiment (Section 4.2.1/Fig. 2) and the incremental-addition experiment (Section 4.2.2/Fig. 3) are creative, targeted demonstrations of the practical benefits of a shared universe (stabilizing poor pairwise correspondences, and cheaply extending the universe to new models), going beyond simply reporting aggregate retrieval numbers.

The theoretical treatment of GCCA as a trace-minimization/spectral problem (Theorem B.1 and corollaries) and the consensus-agreement identity (Proposition 3.2) provide some formal grounding for the proposed correction step, connecting per-sample consensus maximization to global pairwise agreement.

The paper includes several forms of robustness/sensitivity analysis (correspondence noise stress test in Section 4.5, hyperparameter sweeps for (τ, λ) in Appendix C), which strengthens confidence that the method is not narrowly tuned to one setting.
weaknesses: The central claim that GCPA 'retains the practical benefits of the shared Procrustes frame' (i.e., preserves geometry useful for stitching) is never directly validated: the stitching/probing experiments in Section 4.2 only compare PW, GPA-ADD, and GPA-REFIT, and never report GCPA's stitching/probing accuracy. Geometric fidelity of GCPA is only assessed indirectly via an angular 'drift' metric in Appendix C.2, which is not itself validated against a downstream stitching or probing task, leaving the core trade-off claim only partially supported.

The GCPA correction mechanism (a shared MLP trained to match a per-sample consensus direction under a trust-region penalty) is fairly heuristic; unlike the GPA and GCCA formulations, it lacks a closed-form or globally optimal characterization, and no theoretical guarantee is given that the trust-penalty formulation actually achieves a principled trade-off between the GCCA and GPA optima, beyond the observation in Proposition 3.2 that increasing per-view agreement to a consensus increases total pairwise agreement (a fairly generic identity).

In the weak-correspondence stress test (Appendix A.1, Fig. 8), GCPA is shown to sometimes underperform GPA and even become unstable for small/poorly matched universes, indicating that the method is not uniformly beneficial and that its behavior under weak or noisy correspondences is not fully characterized or theoretically explained beyond a qualitative discussion.

The clustering experiment (Section 4.3) shows the odd result that GPA and GCCA barely differ from no-alignment baselines (NA) on ARI/NMI, which is surprising given that both methods are designed to align representations; this counter-intuitive result is not explained in depth, raising questions about whether the clustering protocol or metric is appropriately sensitive to the type of alignment being tested.

No comparisons are made against more expressive alignment baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., functional/spectral alignment methods such as Fumero et al. 2024, or Cannistraci et al.), which would help contextualize how much of GCPA's improvement stems from the multi-way universe formulation versus more general nonlinear alignment capacity.

Reported retrieval results (Tables 2, 3, Figures 4, 6, 7) generally lack confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing, apart from the clustering results in Table 1; this makes it harder to assess whether the (sometimes modest) margins between GCPA and GCCA/GPA are robust rather than due to noise in the correspondence sets or random initialization of Tθ.

Key implementation details for GCPA's correction network (architecture, training schedule, sensitivity to initialization) are relegated to brief appendix descriptions, and the specific values of the fixed (τ, λ) used for the 'dataset-agnostic' configuration are not clearly stated in the main text, limiting exact reproducibility without consulting the provided code.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored issue: most representation-alignment pipelines are pairwise, and a shared-universe/object-to-universe view (GPA-based) is a sensible and clearly motivated alternative that reduces complexity from O(M^2) to O(M) and could, in principle, enforce cycle consistency.

The empirical scope is broad, spanning probing/stitching (CIFAR-100), clustering (MASSIVE, 10 multilingual encoders), cross-lingual retrieval (TED-Multi, with scaling and correspondence-noise stress tests), cross-camera re-identification (Market-1501), and cross-modal retrieval (Flickr8k audio/image/text), which gives the empirical claims reasonable breadth.

The paper is clearly written and the trade-off it investigates (geometry preservation vs. agreement maximization) is intuitive and well illustrated with concrete numbers (e.g., HuBERT→DINOv2/CLIP retrieval gains).
Useful diagnostic analyses are included, such as the incremental model-addition experiment (GPA-ADD vs. GPA-REFIT vs. PW) and the drift/sensitivity ablations for the trust-region hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: GPA is a 1966/1975-era classical technique merely re-applied to neural representations, and GCCA is likewise a long-established multiset method used as a baseline/motivator; the actual proposed contribution (GCPA) is a fairly ad hoc post-hoc MLP correction toward a per-sample consensus direction regularized by an empirically-tuned trust threshold, which is a small increment rather than a principled new alignment objective.

The theoretical content is thin relative to its presentation: Theorem B.1 largely reproduces the standard GCCA spectral solution (already known in the cited literature, e.g., Kettenring 1971; Sorensen et al. 2021), and Proposition 3.2 is essentially an elementary algebraic identity (sum of pairwise cosine similarities as a function of the resultant vector norm) that does not provide non-trivial guarantees about GCPA's actual learned correction (which uses an MLP and a thresholded trust penalty, not the simple linear nudge analyzed in the proposition).

A core selling point of the universe framework is "cycle consistency by design" (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 1, Contribution list), yet the best-performing variant, GCPA, explicitly breaks this property because the learned correction Tθ is not orthogonal (acknowledged directly in Appendix E: "strict orthogonal cycle consistency need not hold after correction"). This undermines the paper's central narrative that a shared universe yields a globally consistent reference, since the empirically superior method sacrifices the very property motivating the universe construction, and this trade-off is not quantified in the main text, only briefly in an appendix.

Some reported comparisons are mathematically close to vacuous: in Table 1, GPA and NA (no alignment) are essentially numerically identical (0.198/0.509 vs 0.198/0.509), which is unsurprising since an orthogonal transform applied independently to each space cannot change intra-space pairwise distances/cosine structure used by k-means; presenting this as an empirical finding rather than acknowledging the algebraic triviality suggests insufficient scrutiny of what the clustering experiment is actually testing.

The baselines compared throughout (PW, GPA, GCCA, GCPA) are all classical/simple linear-algebraic techniques; the paper does not compare against more recent, directly relevant alignment methods it cites in related work (e.g., relative representations, latent functional maps, semantic alignment via Procrustes variants), leaving it unclear whether GCPA's gains would persist against stronger, more modern baselines.

Several experimental setups rely on small or customized benchmarks (synthetic edge-corrupted CIFAR-100 fragile pair, subsampled Market-1501 with only 4 cameras and identity-level rather than image-level correspondence) without statistical significance testing (confidence intervals/seeds) for most retrieval tables, making it hard to judge robustness of the reported margins.

The method requires additional hyperparameters (τ, λ, MLP architecture, training schedule) that are fixed heuristically ("a single conservative (τ, λ) for all experiments"); while a sensitivity sweep is shown, there is no ablation removing the trust penalty entirely or comparing against simpler correction baselines (e.g., a single global linear correction instead of an MLP) to isolate which design choices actually drive the gains.

The paper's own appendix (A.1) shows GCPA can underperform GPA when correspondences are weak/noisy, which is an honest limitation but is in tension with the main narrative of GCPA being a uniformly "best of both worlds" solution.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant gap: most representation-alignment pipelines are pairwise and lack a consistent global reference when more than two models are involved. The paper clearly articulates why this matters (quadratic scaling, cycle-inconsistency) and proposes a sensible universe-factorization fix via GPA.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation spanning stitching/probing (CIFAR-100), clustering (MASSIVE), multilingual retrieval (TED-Multi, including scaling to M=10 languages and a correspondence-noise stress test), cross-camera re-identification (Market-1501), and cross-modal retrieval (Flickr8k with image/text/audio). This breadth strengthens confidence that the GPA vs. GCCA trade-off and the GCPA fix generalize across settings.

The paper identifies and empirically substantiates a clear, intuitive trade-off (geometry preservation vs. retrieval/agreement performance) and backs it with a supporting theoretical analysis (Proposition 3.1 on GCCA's optimality, Proposition 3.2 relating consensus alignment to pairwise agreement, with full proofs in the appendix).

Useful practical demonstrations beyond raw performance numbers: incremental model addition (GPA-ADD vs. REFIT), the "healing weak links" experiment, hyperparameter sensitivity sweeps, and geometry-drift quantification for GCPA, which together give a reasonably thorough picture of the method's behavior and limitations.

Reasonably honest limitations discussion, e.g., noting that GCPA can underperform with very few/weak anchor models (Fig. 8) and that it sacrifices strict orthogonality/cycle-consistency for improved agreement.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is modest: GPA is a long-established classical method (Schönemann 1966; Gower 1975) and its application here is a fairly direct adaptation; GCPA is essentially GPA followed by an MLP that nudges unit directions toward a per-sample centroid with a soft trust-region penalty. The theoretical propositions (3.1, 3.2) are largely known/straightforward facts (GCCA's spectral optimality, a Cauchy-Schwarz-type identity relating consensus alignment to pairwise cosine similarity) rather than deep new insights.

GCPA explicitly breaks the orthogonality/cycle-consistency property that the paper uses as its central motivating advantage of the universe formulation over pairwise alignment (Section 3.1, Appendix E). The paper does not rigorously quantify how much cycle-consistency is lost in the corrected universe in the main experiments (only an aggregate "drift" ablation on one dataset), which undercuts one of the paper's stated selling points when GCPA is used.

The clustering baseline results in Table 1 are curious: GPA and GCCA yield almost identical ARI/NMI to no-alignment (NA) in all three decimal places, which is somewhat suspicious and not explained in depth — e.g., whether this reflects orthogonal transforms being irrelevant to Euclidean-distance-based k-means on standardized features is only alluded to, not analyzed carefully. This weakens confidence that the comparison is fully fair/informative.

Missing comparisons to more recent/competitive alignment baselines mentioned in Related Work but never benchmarked (e.g., Latent Functional Maps, Wasserstein Procrustes, relative representations), making it hard to judge how GCPA stacks up against the current state of the art beyond GPA/GCCA/pairwise.

Hyperparameters (τ, λ) for GCPA are fixed dataset-agnostically, but the sensitivity sweep (Appendix C.1) shows non-trivial variation in mAP (e.g., ~18.3 to ~21.6), and no principled method for choosing them is proposed; reliance on manual tuning limits the method's claimed robustness and reproducibility.

Several results lack variance/significance reporting (e.g., Table 2, Figures 4, 6, 7 appear to report single-run point estimates without confidence intervals), making it difficult to assess the statistical reliability of the reported gains, especially where margins over GCCA are small (e.g., Table 2 M=10 average 0.503 vs. 0.487).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: extending representation alignment from the pairwise setting to M≥3 models via a shared 'universe,' which reduces map complexity from O(M^2) to O(M) and enforces cycle consistency by construction.

Very broad empirical evaluation spanning probing/stitching (CIFAR-100), clustering (MASSIVE, 10 multilingual models), cross-lingual retrieval (TED-MULTI), cross-camera re-identification (MARKET-1501), and cross-modal retrieval (FLICKR8K/30K), with consistent trends across domains supporting the central GPA-vs-GCCA tradeoff and GCPA's improvement.

Extensive and honest ablation studies: sensitivity to hyperparameters (τ, λ), robustness to correspondence noise and test-time feature perturbation, incremental/continual model addition, computational cost analysis, and a 'weak-consensus' failure case where GCPA is shown to underperform GPA, which is a commendable transparent limitation.

The identity in Proposition 3.2 and the closed-form GCCA solution (Theorem B.1) give some formal grounding connecting the consensus-based correction to the sum of pairwise agreements, clarifying the intuition behind why nudging toward the mean direction increases cross-space agreement.

Clear practical utility: the ability to add new models cheaply (GPA-ADD near GPA-REFIT) and to 'heal' weak pairwise links by routing through a multi-model universe is a nice demonstrated use case with direct relevance to model merging/decentralized learning settings.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is modest: GPA is a classical technique (Gower, 1975; Schönemann, 1966) applied essentially off-the-shelf, GCCA is likewise a well-established multiset method, and GCPA itself is a fairly ad hoc post-hoc correction (a small MLP trained with a cosine-consensus loss and a trust-region penalty) rather than a principled, theoretically justified algorithm; Theorem B.1 restates known GCCA optimality results without directly justifying GCPA's own optimality or convergence properties.

No comparisons against genuinely competitive/SOTA methods in each application domain (e.g., established multilingual sentence retrieval models, supervised or state-of-the-art person re-ID cross-camera methods, or existing alignment techniques mentioned in related work such as Relative Representations or Latent Functional Maps); all comparisons are confined to the paper's own baseline family (NA/PW/GPA/GCCA/GCPA), making it hard to judge true significance of the reported gains.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: architecture, training details (optimizer, learning rate, epochs, MLP size) for the GCPA correction network Tθ are not specified in the main text and appear largely absent from the appendix, and the 'fixed dataset-agnostic' (τ, λ) values are never explicitly reported, limiting exact reproducibility.

Some results undercut the narrative without full resolution: GPA fails to improve clustering at all over no alignment (Table 1), and GCPA can underperform GPA when the multi-model consensus is unreliable (Appendix A.1/C7), suggesting the method's benefits are fairly context-dependent and the underlying mechanism for when/why correction helps vs. hurts is only empirically characterized, not theoretically predicted.

Statistical rigor is uneven: variance/seed analysis is reported only for GCPA (Appendix A.7) and not for GCCA or GPA baselines in the main results tables, so it is unclear whether reported margins (e.g., in Tables 1–3) are robust to baseline stochasticity as well.

The retrieval numbers in some settings (e.g., person re-ID mAP, multilingual rank-1) are substantially below typical benchmarks reported elsewhere in the literature for related tasks, and the paper does not contextualize why (e.g., zero-shot camera-level translation without direct image correspondence, weak base encoders), which could give an inflated impression of the practical retrieval performance achieved.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically motivated problem: extending pairwise Procrustes-style representation alignment to the M-way (M≥3) regime, and clearly articulates the scaling and cycle-consistency problems with pairwise approaches.

The experimental breadth is substantial, covering probing/stitching, clustering, and retrieval across multiple modalities and domains (CIFAR-100, MASSIVE, TED-Multi, Market-1501, Flickr8k/30k), which gives the empirical claims some generality.

Numerous robustness and ablation studies are included in the appendix (correspondence noise, weak-consensus failure mode, incremental/continual addition, hyperparameter sensitivity, computational cost, spectral/geometric analysis of the corrected universe), showing an attempt at thorough self-scrutiny.

The GPA-based universe construction is a sensible and clean formalization that reduces map complexity from O(M^2) to O(M) and gives exact cycle consistency for the isometric case, which is a useful engineering contribution even if not deeply novel.
weaknesses: The core novel contribution (GCPA) rests on thin theoretical justification: Proposition 3.2 is a nearly trivial algebraic identity relating sum-of-squared-norms to pairwise cosine similarities, and does not actually justify why nudging toward the per-sample mean direction is a principled or safe correction for retrieval versus simply an averaging/denoising heuristic; GCCA's own optimality (Theorem B.1) is a standard restatement of classical multivariate statistics (Kettenring/Horst-era GCCA) with no new theoretical content specific to representation alignment.

The consensus direction used by GCPA is literally the mean of matched-sample directions across models, i.e., an ensembling/denoising operation. Since evaluation uses the *same* underlying samples across spaces, part of the reported gains (e.g., the large clustering improvement in Table 1, where GPA and GCCA show *zero* improvement over no alignment) could plausibly be explained by simple cross-model averaging denoising rather than a genuine geometric/alignment insight; the paper does not include an ablation isolating the MLP correction from a simple 'project toward consensus centroid' baseline, leaving this confound unaddressed.

The paper's own motivating narrative (Figure 1, Introduction) emphasizes that pairwise methods fail because compositions are not cycle-consistent, and that a shared universe 'guarantees cycle consistency by design.' However, the best-performing method (GCPA) explicitly abandons this guarantee (Appendix D: 'strict orthogonal cycle consistency need not hold after correction'), undercutting the central selling point used to justify the framework.

The proposed correction module (Eq. 8/11–13) uses a trust-region penalty with two hyperparameters (τ, λ) that are fixed heuristically across all experiments; while sensitivity sweeps are shown, the results in Appendix A.1/A.2 demonstrate that GCPA can meaningfully *underperform* GPA when the multi-model consensus is not well-supported, indicating the method's practical reliability is fragile and dataset/composition-dependent, which weakens claims of a generally 'state-of-the-art' method.

Despite an extensive related-work section citing many recent and more expressive alignment methods (Latent Functional Maps, relative representations, ASIF, Wasserstein Procrustes, product-of-invariances, TRIANGLE, etc.), the empirical comparisons are restricted to only pairwise orthogonal Procrustes, GPA, and (G)CCA. None of the more sophisticated recently proposed alignment techniques discussed in Section 2 are benchmarked, so the 'state-of-the-art' claims in the abstract/conclusion are not well supported against the actual current landscape of alignment methods.

Efficiency claims (moving from O(M^2) to O(M) maps) are partially undercut by the reported computational costs in Appendix A.6, where fitting GCPA costs 2-5x the runtime of GPA and more memory, without a clear discussion of how this scales with very large M or feature dimension in realistic deployment settings.

Most main-text figures/tables (Fig. 2-4, 6-7) report point estimates without confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; variability analysis is deferred to a limited appendix study (10 seeds on 3 benchmarks), making it hard to assess whether the often modest margins over GCCA in the main results (e.g., Table 2, Table 3) are robust.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant limitation of pairwise representation alignment (quadratic scaling, lack of cycle consistency) and offers a coherent shared-universe factorization solution with clear complexity benefits (O(M) vs O(M^2)).

Extensive and diverse experimental validation spanning inter-architecture probing/stitching, clustering (MASSIVE), multilingual retrieval (TED-MULTI), cross-camera re-identification (MARKET-1501), and multimodal retrieval (FLICKR8K/30K), with consistent trends across settings supporting the central claim that GCPA balances geometric fidelity and retrieval performance.

Solid theoretical grounding for the GCCA baseline (Theorem B.1 and corollaries) and a clean identity (Proposition 3.2) linking per-sample consensus alignment to total pairwise agreement, which motivates the design of the GCPA correction objective.

Very thorough robustness and ablation studies (hyperparameter sensitivity, correspondence noise, test-time feature noise, incremental/continual model addition, model-choice/composition analysis, multi-seed variability, dimension-matching strategies), reflecting careful empirical rigor.

Commendably honest treatment of limitations, including an explicit 'weak-consensus' experiment showing GCPA can underperform GPA when correspondences are unreliable, and a discussion of when each method (GPA vs. GCCA vs. GCPA) is preferable rather than overclaiming universal superiority.
weaknesses: The core novel component, GCPA, is a fairly heuristic add-on (a shared MLP nudging directions toward a consensus, with a soft trust-region penalty) rather than a principled objective with optimality guarantees; the theoretical results (Prop. 3.1, 3.2) largely restate/adapt classical facts about GCCA and cosine consensus, offering limited additional insight into why the specific GCPA construction is the right way to bridge the isometry-agreement gap.

GCPA relaxes strict orthogonality, so it loses the exact cycle-consistency property that is prominently advertised as a key motivation for the universe factorization in the introduction; this tension between the stated core contribution (consistent composable reference) and the best-performing method (which sacrifices that property) is somewhat underexplored in the main text.

Key algorithmic details (full GCPA and GCCA procedures) are deferred entirely to appendices D and E, making the main text's methodological description incomplete for a reader trying to assess exact reproducibility without consulting extensive appendices.

The 'fixed, dataset-agnostic' GCPA hyperparameter configuration used for all main results is not fully justified in terms of how it was selected without implicit tuning on the evaluation benchmarks, which could raise fairness-of-comparison concerns relative to GPA/GCCA baselines.

The method's benefits and applicability are somewhat narrow in scope (linear/orthogonal + shallow MLP correction), and the paper explicitly defers more expressive non-isometric multi-way alignment to future work, limiting the generality of the contribution to more heterogeneous or nonlinear model collections.
